title: The oak and the reeds
hookLine: the oak breaks in the storm, and the reeds bend and live (Aesop)

cards: A storm is coming over a river valley. The sky goes green, the wind gets loud, and everything standing up has to decide what to do about it.
On the bank there's a huge oak, the kind of tree people have picnics under, the kind that looks like it will outlast everyone.
And down at the water's edge there's a patch of reeds, thin as pencils, the kind nobody notices. The smart money is on the oak. The people who told this story counted on that.

teach.b: It's another of Aesop's fables, and it comes down in more than one version, with one reed or many. Here's one telling. A great wind tears through the valley.
The oak stands firm, because that's what oaks do. The wind keeps pushing, and the oak keeps refusing, until with a crack its roots rip out of the bank and it falls into the river.
The current carries it downstream, past the reeds, a little ruffled, and fine. The oak asks how they survived, when something so small should have been flattened.
And the reeds answer, more or less: you fought the wind, and it broke you. We bowed our heads, and let it pass over us. Look at what that answer isn't.

teach.h: THE REEDS BOW, AND STAND AGAIN.
teach.b: The reeds didn't stop being reeds. When the storm moved on, they stood straight again, rooted in the same mud. Bending isn't the same as being blown away.
And the oak's strength was real, and admirable, and no use in this one storm, because it had only one move. Some old versions add a moral: those who yield to what they can't fight come through it.
Another reading is quieter. A few things in life are worth standing against.

teach.h: MOST OF A DAY'S WIND ISN'T WORTH IT.
teach.b: Most of what blows through an ordinary day isn't. A plan changed at the last minute is wind. The way someone loads the dishwasher is wind.

how: People who read Aesop as everyday wisdom often reach for the oak and the reeds when they talk about flexibility: letting small things pass while keeping one's roots.

o: tall grasses that grow in dry fields
young trees planted along a riverbank
tall thin water plants that bend in the wind

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: stands firm, and is torn out
bow and let the wind pass
how did something so small survive?

s: the reeds stop being reeds to survive
they bow while the storm passes, then stand straight again in the same mud.
the oak asks the reeds how they survived
and they answer: you fought the wind, and it broke you; we bowed, and let it pass.
some old versions add a moral at the end
that those who yield to what they can't fight come through it.

games.q: you're the reeds. the storm is here, and the wind is roaring. what do you do?
o: stand tall and fight it, like the oak
bow your heads and let it pass over
let go of the bank and float away
games.why: they bow. the oak stands, is torn out, and floats downstream past them. afterward the reeds stand up again where they were.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing you've been holding stiff about, a plan someone changed, a habit of someone you live with, a word that bugs you, and notice where you hold it in your body, maybe the jaw, maybe the shoulders.
Picture the reeds at the water's edge, bowing as the wind goes over, and on each out-breath, let that place bend a little. You're not giving up who you are; you're letting one gust pass.

wordCard.voice: reeds. Thin stems that bow, let the storm pass, and stand up again, while the strong oak that fought it breaks.

orig.note: Greek: reed. the fables come down to us in Greek, and this is the plant that bends.

carryVoice: Your line: bend, don't break. Rooted in the same mud, and still able to bow. See you tomorrow.
